transcript.text: Welcome to On Print Shop.
In this tutorial we'll walk you through how to prepare 3D product models for use in our designer studio.
You'll learn how to set up materials, define print areas, apply textures, use UV mapping, and finally export the model in a web friendly format.
We'll begin with AT Shirt example and then move on to a mug so you'll see how the same workflow can be adapted to different product types.
Please note the base 3D models themselves, such as the T-shirt you'll see here, are usually created in specialized software like Marvelous Designer for realistic garment modeling.
Our focus today is on preparing those models inside Blender and integrating them seamlessly with Designer Studio.
Let's first look at the Polo T-shirt inside Designer Studio.
This product comes with multiple print areas, front pocket, left sleeve, right sleeve and the back.
Each area has defined print dimensions so customers can upload separate designs for each part.
They can also so change the T-shirts base color dynamically, creating a truly personalized product preview.
Now let's prepare this T-shirt in Blender.
For every print area, we need to define it carefully.
This is done by duplicating the relevant part of the mesh to isolate that print zone and positioning it according to the exact product dimensions.
Next, unwrap the Uvs of the print areas.
First select the edges around the print area.
Then go to the UV menu and click Mark Seam.
The edges will turn red.
After that, select all the faces of the print area, go back to the UV menu and choose Project from View to unwrap.
This method is simple and works well here, but in some cases you can just mark seams and use a regular unwrap instead to create materials for all the sides and apply a placeholder image.
Your design here.
A template image can then be created in Photoshop or similar software with the correct size, for example 4.5 cross 5 inches for the pocket.
To ensure everything blends smoothly, PNG images with transparent backgrounds are used for print zones.
Go to Shader Editor, apply the image in Image Texture and connect the color node to Base color.
As the image is PNG, the alpha node of Image Texture should be connected to alpha node of the principal BSDF, allowing the print areas to blend naturally with the base color underneath.
To make the T-shirt look realistic, we also apply a fabric material.
A seamless cotton fabric texture can be imported and can be baked in Blender to use as the base material.
A normal map is then added to simulate surface detail.
Next is to name the textures for all the print areas.
For example, for the front pocket, we have named it Front Pocket_texture the_texture.
Part is crucial for the studio to recognize the textures correctly now go.
To the UV editor AND adjust the uvs to Align correctly with the image placed in the placeholder make sure.
That Uvs are Properly scaled and ositioned.
This ensures the design preview appears accurately in Designer Studio.
To begin the UV mapping process for a multi print polo shirt, the first step is to select and combine the relevant print areas.
In this example, the back, right sleeve, left sleeve and front pocket are selected and then combined to create a unified layout for UV mapping.
After combining, the materials section displays the individual materials corresponding to each print area, front pocket, left sleeve, right sleeve and back.
These materials are organized in the correct order, making it easier to select the mesh and assign UV maps accordingly.
In Designer Studio, the print pages are arranged in a specific sequence, front, left sleeve, right sleeve, and back.
To ensure proper alignment, the UV maps must be set in the same order.
This is why the print areas are combined following the sequence.
Next, the mesh for each print area is selected within its respective material for each material, starting with Front Pocket.
To add UV maps, navigate to the Data tab in the Properties panel, go to UV Maps and click the Plus icon.
This adds the selected UV map and names it accordingly, for example, front for the Front Pocket area.
Repeat this process for all print areas, left sleeve, right sleeve, and back, maintaining the same order as defined in Designer Studio.
After all UV maps are added, select the first EV map default.
Keeping the UV maps in the correct order is important as it ensures that any print placed on a specific page will appear in the correct location on the 3D model during preview.
Moving to the color element, for the base T-shirt color, we use a separate material ending with_color, for example, shirt base_color.
This convention allows customers to dynamically change colors in Designer Studio.
Now let's move on to a mug model.
While the workflow is similar, the material and print setups are slightly different.
Since mugs are ceramic, the material should have low roughness to achieve a shiny reflective surface.
A normal map can be added if subtle surface effects are desired.
The print areas are defined based on the mug type, whether it's a full wrap around design or just a centered logo.
As with AT shirt, the mesh is duplicated for the print area, UV unwrapped and assigned materials with proper mapping.
The same_texture and_color naming conventions apply here as well.
For mugs, the print area dimensions are usually based on the mug size, often measured in ounces such as 11 oz or 15 ounces.
Once the model is ready, in the 3D viewport, click on the object or objects you want to export.
At the top menu, click File, then Export, then DLTF 2.0 dot DLB or dot DLTF.
In the Export window, select the file format GLTF with separate dot bin and texture files.
Tick Selected objects to export only what you selected.
Tick Custom Properties.
Tick Apply Modifiers to apply any modifiers.
Tick UV's and Normals for correct texture and shading information, Choose where to save your file and give it a name, and finally, click Export GLTF 2.0 to finish.
And that's it.
You've learned how to prepare T-shirt and mug models for Designer Studio, covering print areas, realistic materials, UV mapping and exporting.
While modeling may start elsewhere, mastering Blender setup ensures your products look great and work perfectly.
Once you are ready with your 3D model, it is time to add and assign the model to its respective product in the On Print Shop admin panel.
To start, log into your admin panel and from the left navigation go to Designer Studio, Studio Settings Reel Preview.
From here, click on the Reel Preview Models button and then select Add to upload a new model.
On the Add Reel Preview Models page, choose the preview type as 3D and enter a suitable title such as Polo T-shirt 3D Model.
Next, set the model type to GLTFGLB.
Upload your GLTFGLB file along with any additional files and configure the environment type to adjust lighting and reflections.
To further enhance the display, enable punctual lights for focused lighting on the model.
Once the model is added, you can assign it to a product.
Go back to the Real Preview main screen and click on the Assign Real Preview Models button.
On the Assign Reel preview page, select the desired product.
For example, pull a shirt under the Men's clothing category and decide whether to assign the model to the entire product size wise or based on product options.
For this example, choose the product option from the drop down list.
Select the 3D model you uploaded, enable the status for the assignment and click Save.
Your 3D model is now added and successfully linked with the product in Designer Studio.
Thank you for watching and we look forward to seeing your amazing 3D products come to life.
